title: Ageing with grace
hookLine: old age as a season, not a loss
tomorrow: Simran's college essay is stuck. who does she ask?

lines: MY HANDS ARE IN THE FOURTH WATCH.
A LIFE TOLD AS ONE NIGHT.
cards: Every feed has an ad that promises to make you look younger. Baba Kartar would not be the target audience. His hands shake now; his tea rattles on the saucer, and Simran, who notices everything, pretends not to.
He doesn't pretend. He lifts the cup, watches it tremble, and says, my hands are in the fourth watch. Then he drinks.
Fourth watch of what? It sounds like a riddle, and it is one. It comes from Guru Nanak, in Sri Raag, Ang 74, in a poem called the Pehre.
And the strange thing is the shape of it: a whole human life, told as one single night.

teach.h: A LIFE TOLD AS ONE NIGHT.
teach.b: Why a night? Guru Nanak divides it into watches, the way a night guard's shift is divided. In the first watch, in paraphrase, the soul arrives by the Command.
In the next, youth, and forgetting. Then the body, and wealth. In the fourth, the reaper comes to the field.
And all the way through he speaks to the listener by an odd, warm name: O my merchant friend. A trader, passing through, with something to trade.
Here's the thing to tell someone tonight: Guru Nanak's poem about growing old calls you his merchant friend in every watch. Now the puzzle's answer. A night isn't a day that went wrong.
It has its own hours and its own work.
The poem doesn't sweeten the fourth watch; the body tires, and the reaper is real.
But the call in the fourth watch is the same as in the first: remember the Name. No watch is too late. None is the wrong one.
Baba Kartar's reading is simple. My hands shake, he says, and they still fold. Each watch has its own work.

how: Sikhs hear the Pehre of Sri Raag read and sung in the Guru Granth Sahib; elders in many Sikh families keep their daily prayers into old age, often reading from a gutka or listening when their eyes tire.

o: growing old as a season with its own work
retiring from every duty to rest at last
staying young-looking for as long as you can

games.q: one night, four watches — tap the pairs.
p: a life told as the watches of a night
the reaper comes to the field

s: in the Pehre, the last watch is too late to remember God
the call is the same in every watch: remember the Name.
Guru Nanak tells a whole life as one night in the Pehre
Sri Raag, Ang 74: the watches of one night, from arrival to the reaper.
growing old means you've lost the best part of the day
a popular view. in the Pehre each watch has its own work.

games.q: your grandmother says she's useless now that she can't cook for the family anymore. what does the Pehre give you to say?
o: you're not useless at all; you look great for your age!
this watch has its own work, like the stories only you know.
rest now; your work is all done and you've earned it.
games.why: in the Pehre no watch is the wrong one. the fourth watch isn't sweetened, but it has its own work.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up. Starting at your feet, give each part of your body a silent thank you for one thing it did today: feet for the walk, hands for the cup, eyes for this screen.
Go slowly, and thank the parts that ache too.

wordCard.voice: Ageing with grace. In Guru Nanak's Pehre, old age is the fourth watch of one night: a season with its own work, not the loss of the day.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pehre, the watches of the night; Guru Nanak's poem of a life as one night.

carryVoice: The line to keep: every season, the fourth watch too, each with its own work. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74-75 (Sri Raag, Pehre, Mahalla 1: the four watches of the night, addressed to the merchant friend), paraphrased
